claim: Wound healing is a fundamental biological process comprising three sequential and overlapping phases: inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling.
source: Wound healing is a fundamental biological process (BP) comprising three sequential and overlapping phases, that is, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling (Reinke and Sorg, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinke and Sorg, 2012

claim: The delicate wound repair process is often disrupted in chronic venous insufficiency patients, resulting in venous ulcers characterized by persistent inflammation and proliferative phase initiation failure.
source: This delicate repair process is often disrupted in chronic venous insufficiency patients, resulting in venous ulcers (VUs) characterized by persistent inflammation and proliferative phase initiation failure (Eming et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eming et al., 2014

claim: VU is the most common chronic nonhealing wound type, comprising 45–60% of all lower extremity ulcerations.
source: VU is the most common chronic nonhealing wound type, comprising 45–60% of all lower extremity ulcerations (Vivas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vivas et al., 2016

claim: VU exhibits a marked impact on health-related life quality and represents a significant financial burden with an annual health care cost of overall $14.9 billion in the USA.
source: VU exhibits a marked impact on health-related life quality and represents a significant financial burden both to the patients and the society with an annual health care cost of overall $14.9 billion in the USA (Hoversten et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoversten et al., 2020

claim: MicroRNAs are short (~22 nt) noncoding ribonucleic acids that incorporate into the RNA-induced silencing complex and bind to the 3′ untranslated region of their target mRNAs, resulting in mRNA destabilization and translational repression.
source: MicroRNAs (miR) represent a group of short (~22 nt) noncoding (nc) ribonucleic acids, incorporating into the RNA-induced silencing complex and binding to the 3′ untranslated region of their target mRNAs, resulting in mRNA destabilization and translational repression (Stavast and Erkeland, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stavast and Erkeland, 2019

claim: An individual miR can target dozens to hundreds of genes.
source: Given that an individual miR can target dozens to hundreds of genes, miRs have been identified as regulators of complex gene networks (Stavast and Erkeland, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stavast and Erkeland, 2019

claim: MiR-mediated regulation is reportedly crucial in multiple fundamental biological processes including skin wound repair.
source: MiR-mediated regulation is reportedly crucial in multiple fundamental BPs including skin wound repair (Herter and Xu Landén, 2017, Meng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herter and Xu Landén, 2017, and Meng et al., 2018

claim: Manipulating miRs critical for disease pathogenesis could offer a prominent therapeutic effect, supported by viral infection- and cancer-targeting miR therapeutics clinical trials.
source: Importantly, manipulating miRs critical for the disease pathogenesis could offer a prominent therapeutic effect, supported by viral infection- and cancer-targeting miR therapeutics clinical trials (Rupaimoole and Slack, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rupaimoole and Slack, 2017

claim: miR-based therapeutics for hard-to-heal wounds represent a promising approach.
source: Therefore, miR-based therapeutics for hard-to-heal wounds represent a promising approach (Herter and Xu Landén, 2017, Luan et al., 2018, Meng et al., 2018; Nie et al., 2020; Pastar et al., 2020, Sen and Roy, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Human skin structure and repair processes are different from those of commonly used animal models (e.g., rodents).
source: Despite sharing several fundamental features, the human skin structure and repair processes are different from those of the commonly used animal models (e.g., rodents) (Elliot et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliot et al., 2018

claim: Animal models cannot fully simulate the human disease complexity, and the findings are difficult to extrapolate to humans.
source: Moreover, animal models cannot fully simulate the human disease complexity, and the findings are difficult to extrapolate to humans (Darwin and Tomic-Canic, 2018; Pastar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Darwin and Tomic-Canic, 2018, and Pastar et al., 2018

claim: The study performed paired small and mRNA expression profiling in human skin, acute wounds during the inflammatory and proliferative phases, and VU.
source: In this study, we performed paired small and mRNA expression profiling in the human skin, acute wounds during the inflammatory and proliferative phases, and VU, unraveling time-resolved changes of the whole transcriptome throughout the wound healing process and the unique gene expression signature of a common chronic wound type.
evidence: Direct statement of the study methodology

claim: The study detected 562 mature miRs and 12,069 mRNAs in the samples.
source: After stringent raw sequencing data quality control (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2), we detected 562 mature miRs and 12,069 mRNAs in our samples.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: Principal component analysis showed that either the miR or the mRNA expression profiles clearly separated the four sample groups (Skin, Wound1, Wound7, and VU).
source: Our principal component analysis showed that either the miR or the mRNA expression profiles clearly separated these four sample groups (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and Figure 1b

claim: The study identified a VU-specific gene signature, including aberrant increase of 22 miRs and 221 mRNAs and decrease of 10 miRs and 203 mRNAs.
source: We compared the VUs with both the skin and acute wounds and unraveled a VU-specific gene signature, including aberrant increase of 22 miRs and 221 mRNAs and decrease of 10 miRs and 203 mRNAs (differentially expressed [DE] analysis false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05, fold change ≥2 for miRs, and ≥1.5 for mRNAs, Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis with specific statistical criteria and figures

claim: The study identified 13 distinct miRNA coexpression modules using WGCNA.
source: We identified 13 distinct modules with a robustness confirmed by the module preservation analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), 10 of them significantly correlating (Pearson's correlation, FDR <0.05) with at least one of the four phenotypic traits, that is, Skin, Wound1, Wound7, and VU (Figure 2a, b, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis and figures

claim: Module m2, m10, and m11 miRs were upregulated at the inflammatory phase (Wound1).
source: The WGCNA revealed that module (m)2, m10, and m11 miRs were upregulated at the inflammatory phase (Wound1), while m5 and m6 miRs peaked at the proliferative phase (Wound7).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis results

claim: Module m5 and m6 miRs peaked at the proliferative phase (Wound7).
source: The WGCNA revealed that module (m)2, m10, and m11 miRs were upregulated at the inflammatory phase (Wound1), while m5 and m6 miRs peaked at the proliferative phase (Wound7).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis results

claim: In VU, three downregulated (m3, m7, and m9) and two upregulated (m8 and m12) miR modules were identified.
source: In VU, we identified three downregulated (m3, m7, and m9) and two upregulated (m8 and m12) miR modules.
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis results

claim: 84% of the 198 'driver' miRs were identified as differentially expressed genes.
source: Notably, we identified 84% of them as DEGs, suggesting a high consistence between the WGCNA and DE analysis (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of WGCNA and differential expression analysis

claim: KLF4, KLF5, GATA3, GRHL2, and TP53 families exhibited their binding sites enriched in the m9 miR genes and their expression significantly correlated with the m9 miRs.
source: Interestingly, the KLF4, KLF5, GATA3, GRHL2, and TP53 families exhibited not only their binding sites enriched in the m9 miR genes but their expression also significantly correlated with the m9 miRs (Pearson's correlation coefficient = 0.53–0.82, p value of p = 7.05e−06–0.014) (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3a, and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis and correlation analysis

claim: Both GATA3 and KLF4 are reportedly downregulated in human VU.
source: Notably, both GATA3 and KLF4 are reportedly downregulated in human VU (Stojadinovic et al., 2014; Stojadinovic et al., 2008), which findings were confirmed in our RNA-seq data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by RNA-seq data

claim: The study identified 13 mRNA coexpression modules using WGCNA.
source: We thus performed WGCNA in the paired long RNA-seq data and identified 13 mRNA coexpression modules (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 4a–c, and Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by WGCNA analysis

claim: The gene ontology analysis of the mRNA modules largely confirmed the previous knowledge of wound biology.
source: The gene ontology (GO) analysis of the mRNA modules largely confirmed the previous knowledge of wound biology, such as skin hemostasis (M2) and barrier function (M4)-related gene downregulation in the wounds, the upregulation of the genes involved in the immune response (M8), RNA processing, and protein production (M1, M3, and M5) in the inflammatory phase, and the prominent cell mitosis-related gene expression (M7) in the proliferative phase of wound repair (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis and comparison with existing knowledge

claim: NFKB1 and RELA were identified as the most enriched upstream regulators for the M1 mRNAs.
source: For example, we identified NFKB1 and RELA, well known for their immune functions (Liu et al., 2017), as the most enriched upstream regulators for the M1 mRNAs, while E2F1, a TF promoting cell growth (Ertosun et al., 2016), surfaced as a master regulator TF in M7 (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis and citations

claim: E2F1 surfaced as a master regulator TF in M7.
source: For example, we identified NFKB1 and RELA, well known for their immune functions (Liu et al., 2017), as the most enriched upstream regulators for the M1 mRNAs, while E2F1, a TF promoting cell growth (Ertosun et al., 2016), surfaced as a master regulator TF in M7 (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: Supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis and citation

claim: The study unraveled a VU molecular signature: downregulated expression of RNA and protein production- (M1, M3, and M5) as well as cell mitosis-related (M7) genes, and upregulated expression of genes involved in extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion (M9).
source: Importantly, our study unraveled a VU molecular signature: downregulated expression of RNA and protein production- (M1, M3, and M5) as well as cell mitosis-related (M7) genes, and upregulated expression of genes involved in extracellular matrix organization and cell adhesion (M9).
evidence: Supported by mRNA module analysis

claim: The study found an immune gene signature clearly distinguishing the chronic inflammation in VUs (M11 and M12 enriched with adaptive immunity-related mRNAs) from the self-limiting immune response in acute wounds (M8 enriched with neutrophil activation- and phagocytosis-related mRNAs).
source: Moreover, we found an immune gene signature clearly distinguishing the chronic inflammation in VUs (M11 and M12 enriched with adaptive immunity-related mRNAs) from the self-limiting immune response in acute wounds (M8 enriched with neutrophil activation- and phagocytosis-related mRNAs) (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: Supported by mRNA module analysis and GO analysis

claim: The study found significantly negative correlations between the PC1 of the DE miRs and the DE mRNAs predicted as miR targets.
source: We found significantly negative correlations (Pearson's correlation, p values: 1.36e−12–1.27e−04) between the PC1 of the DE miRs and the DE mRNAs predicted as miR targets, indicating negative regulation of VU-mRNA signature by the aberrantly expressed miRs in VU (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: The study identified significantly negative correlations between the downregulated miR (m3, m7, and m9) and the upregulated mRNA (M9, M11, and M12) modules in VU.
source: We identified significantly negative correlations between the downregulated miR (m3, m7, and m9) and the upregulated mRNA (M9, M11, and M12) modules, as well as between the upregulated miR (m8 and m12) and the downregulated mRNA (M5) modules in VU (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between miR and mRNA modules

claim: The predicted targets of the downregulated m9 miRs were significantly enriched for the upregulated M9 mRNAs.
source: Among these miR–mRNA module pairs, we found that the predicted targets of the downregulated m9 miRs were significantly enriched (Fisher's extract test: OR >1, p value <0.05) for the upregulated M9 mRNAs, whereas the targets of the upregulated miRs and m8 miRs were enriched for the downregulated mRNAs and M5 mRNAs (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis

claim: The targets of the upregulated miRs and m8 miRs were enriched for the downregulated mRNAs and M5 mRNAs.
source: Among these miR–mRNA module pairs, we found that the predicted targets of the downregulated m9 miRs were significantly enriched (Fisher's extract test: OR >1, p value <0.05) for the upregulated M9 mRNAs, whereas the targets of the upregulated miRs and m8 miRs were enriched for the downregulated mRNAs and M5 mRNAs (Figure 4a and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis

claim: The study identified 17 pathologically relevant miRs that exhibited abnormal VU expression and displayed their targets enriched explicitly in the VU gene signature.
source: With this first clinical, wound-centric resource of miRs and mRNAs, we identified 17 pathologically relevant miRs that exhibited abnormal VU expression and displayed their targets enriched explicitly in the VU gene signature.
evidence: Supported by integrative analysis of miR and mRNA expression

claim: The study validated the expression of 11 miRs by qRT-PCR in a cohort with 7 healthy donors and 12 VU patients.
source: First, we selected 9 shortlisted DE miRs (Figures 1d and 4b), including 3 downregulated (miR-149-5p, miR-218-5p, and miR-96-5p) and 6 upregulated (miR-7704, miR-424-5p, miR-31-3p, miR-450-5p, miR-516b-5p, and miR-517b-3p) miRs in VU, and validated their expression by quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) in the skin and wound tissue biopsies from a cohort with 7 healthy donors and 12 VU patients, matched in terms of age and the anatomical wound locations (Figure 5b–j, Tables 1 and 2, and Figure 5—source data 1). Additionally, the upregulation of miR-34a-5p and miR-34c-5p in VU has been reported by us previously (Wu et al., 2020). Together, we confirmed these 11 miRs' expression patterns in RNA-seq, supporting the robustness and reproducibility of our profiling data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR validation and previous publication

claim: The expression of miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p was upregulated in the wound-edge epidermis from the VUs compared to the acute wounds and the skin.
source: In addition, with laser capture microdissection (LCM), we isolated the epidermal compartments from human skin, acute wounds, and VUs (n = 7 per group) and found that the expression of miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p was upregulated in the wound-edge epidermis from the VUs compared to the acute wounds and the skin, as shown in qRT-PCR analysis (Figure 5l–n).
evidence: Supported by LCM and qRT-PCR analysis

claim: For all eight miRs tested, the strongest targets predicted by TargetScan were significantly downregulated compared to the nontargeting mRNAs in microarray analysis.
source: For all these eight miRs, we observed that their strongest targets predicted by TargetScan were significantly downregulated compared to the nontargeting mRNAs (Wilcoxon t-test p values: 1.34e−25–1.91e−59).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis and statistical testing

claim: The experimentally validated miR-218-5p, miR-34a-5p, miR-34c-5p, and miR-7704 targets showed significant enrichment for the VU gene signature.
source: Notably, we observed significant enrichment (Fisher's exact test, OR >1, p value <0.05) of the experimentally validated miR-218-5p, miR-34a-5p, miR-34c-5p, and miR-7704 targets for the VU gene signature (Figure 6k and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of validated targets

claim: miR-34a and miR-34c inhibit keratinocyte proliferation and migration, while promoting apoptosis and inflammatory response, resulting in delayed wound repair in a mouse model.
source: We have previously shown that miR-34a and miR-34c inhibit keratinocyte proliferation and migration, while promoting apoptosis and inflammatory response, resulting in delayed wound repair in a mouse model (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication

claim: Both the predicted and validated miR-34a/c targets were enriched for the downregulated M5 module mRNAs in VU.
source: Here, we discovered that both the predicted (Figure 4b) and validated (Figure 6k) miR-34a/c targets were enriched for the downregulated M5 module mRNAs in VU.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of predicted and validated targets

claim: miR-34a or miR-34c overexpression reduced the expression of 39 hub genes in the M5 module in cultured keratinocytes.
source: Notably, our microarray analysis in cultured keratinocytes overexpressing miR-34a or miR-34c confirmed that miR-34 reduced the expression of 39 hub genes in the M5 module (log2(fold change) ≤−0.58, p value <0.05, Figure 7a, lower panel), and 26 of them exhibited negative correlation (Pearson's r = −0.83 to −0.45, p value <0.05) with miR-34a/c expression levels in the human skin and wound samples (Figure 7a, upper panel and Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that they were miR-34a/c targets in vivo.
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis and correlation analysis

claim: miR-218-5p was downregulated in the VU compared to the acute wounds and the skin.
source: MiR-218-5p was downregulated in the VU compared to the acute wounds and the skin (Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis

claim: The predicted and validated targets of miR-218-5p were both enriched for the upregulated or M9 module mRNAs in VU.
source: Its predicted (Figure 4b) and validated (Figure 7a) targets were both enriched for the upregulated or M9 module mRNAs in VU.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis

claim: miR-7704 is a human-specific miR with significantly increased expression in VU.
source: Interestingly, this study also identified miR-7704, a human-specific miR, with significantly increased expression in VU (Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis

claim: The predicted and validated miR-7704 targets were highly enriched for the M5 module mRNAs downregulated in VU.
source: Similar to miR-34a/c, the predicted (Figure 4b) and validated (Figure 6k) miR-7704 targets were highly enriched for the M5 module mRNAs downregulated in VU.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis

claim: miR-34a/c and miR-424-5p or miR-7704 shared 8–10 targets with unrelated seed sequences.
source: For the miRs with unrelated seed sequences, we found that miR-34a/c and miR-424-5p or miR-7704 shared 8–10 targets, and these miRs were coexpressed in the m8 module.
evidence: Supported by target analysis and coexpression analysis

claim: Among the downregulated miRs in VU, miR-96-5p and miR-218-5p shared eight targets.
source: We showed that among the downregulated miRs in VU, miR-96-5p and miR-218-5p shared eight targets.
evidence: Supported by target analysis

claim: The miRs upregulated in VU (miR-34a-5p, miR-34c-5p, miR-424-5p, miR-450-5p, miR-7704, and miR-516-5p) were predicted to promote inflammation but inhibit proliferation.
source: Of particular interest, combining the miR expression changes with their annotated functions, we found a regular pattern, that is, the miRs upregulated in VU (i.e., miR-34a-5p, miR-34c-5p, miR-424-5p, miR-450-5p, miR-7704, and miR-516-5p) were predicted to promote inflammation but inhibit proliferation; whereas the miRs downregulated in VU (i.e., miR-218-5p and miR-96-5p) might be required for cell growth and activation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by functional annotation analysis

claim: The miRs downregulated in VU (miR-218-5p and miR-96-5p) might be required for cell growth and activation.
source: Of particular interest, combining the miR expression changes with their annotated functions, we found a regular pattern, that is, the miRs upregulated in VU (i.e., miR-34a-5p, miR-34c-5p, miR-424-5p, miR-450-5p, miR-7704, and miR-516-5p) were predicted to promote inflammation but inhibit proliferation; whereas the miRs downregulated in VU (i.e., miR-218-5p and miR-96-5p) might be required for cell growth and activation (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by functional annotation analysis

claim: VU-dysregulated miRs might cooperatively result in impaired cell migration and proliferation accompanied with persistent inflammation, contributing to the stalled wound healing characterized with failed transition from the inflammatory phase to the proliferative phase.
source: Therefore, these VU-dysregulated miRs might cooperatively result in impaired cell migration and proliferation accompanied with persistent inflammation, contributing to the stalled wound healing characterized with failed transition from the inflammatory phase to the proliferative phase (Landén et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference from functional annotation analysis and citation

claim: miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p cooperatively suppressed keratinocyte proliferation.
source: We found that although miR-34a-5p or miR-424-5p alone could reduce Ki-67 levels, their combination suppressed stronger Ki-67 expression (Figure 9a, b, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, and Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on Ki-67 expression

claim: The cooperativity between miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p in repressing keratinocyte growth was confirmed by comparing cell growth curves generated with a live cell imaging system.
source: The cooperativity between miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p in repressing keratinocyte growth was further confirmed by comparing cell growth curves generated with a live cell imaging system (Figure 9c, Figure 9—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 9—video 1).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p delayed keratinocyte migration.
source: Next, with scratch wound healing assays, we showed that simultaneous overexpression of miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p delayed keratinocyte migration, whereas inhibition of endogenous miR-34a-5p or miR-424-5p enhanced keratinocyte motility (Figure 9d–g).
evidence: Supported by scratch wound healing assay data

claim: Inhibition of endogenous miR-34a-5p or miR-424-5p enhanced keratinocyte motility.
source: Next, with scratch wound healing assays, we showed that simultaneous overexpression of miR-34a-5p and miR-424-5p delayed keratinocyte migration, whereas inhibition of endogenous miR-34a-5p or miR-424-5p enhanced keratinocyte motility (Figure 9d–g).
evidence: Supported by scratch wound healing assay data

claim: Simultaneously overexpressing miR-34a-5p and miR-516b-5p induced a higher CCL20 expression compared to the individual overexpression of each miR.
source: We showed that simultaneously overexpressing miR-34a-5p and miR-516b-5p induced a higher CCL20 expression compared to the individual overexpression of each miR, suggesting their cooperativity in promoting inflammation (Figure 9h).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data on CCL20 expression

claim: The study developed a compendium (https://www.xulandenlab.com/humanwounds-mirna-mrna), which is an open, comprehensive resource to broadly aid wound healing research.
source: On the basis of the findings, we developed a compendium (https://www.xulandenlab.com/humanwounds-mirna-mrna), which will be an open, comprehensive resource to broadly aid wound healing research.
evidence: Direct statement about the resource development

claim: The study demonstrated that miR-34a, miR-424, and miR-516, upregulated in VU, cooperatively suppressed keratinocyte migration and growth while promoting inflammatory response.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that miR-34a, miR-424, and miR-516, upregulated in VU, cooperatively suppressed keratinocyte migration and growth while promoting inflammatory response.
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data

claim: The study opens the possibility of developing innovative wound treatment that targets pathologically relevant cooperating miRs to attain higher therapeutic efficacy and specificity.
source: Our study opens the possibility of developing innovative wound treatment that targets pathologically relevant cooperating miRs to attain higher therapeutic efficacy and specificity.
evidence: Inference from the study findings

claim: The same miR is often described to play different or even opposite roles in different cells, as each cell type has specific gene expression context subjected to the miR-mediated posttranscriptional regulation.
source: The same miR is often described to play different or even opposite roles in different cells, as each cell type has specific gene expression context subjected to the miR-mediated posttranscriptional regulation (Erhard et al., 2014).

claim: miR-34a was identified as one of the most induced miRs in diabetic foot ulcer fibroblasts.
source: miR-34a was also identified as one of the most induced miRs in diabetic foot ulcer fibroblasts. Induction of miR-34a together with miR‐21‐5p and miR‐145‐5p inhibits fibroblast movement and proliferation, whereas activates cell differentiation and senescence (Liang et al., 2016).

claim: Induction of miR-34a together with miR‐21‐5p and miR‐145‐5p inhibits fibroblast movement and proliferation, whereas activates cell differentiation and senescence.
source: Induction of miR-34a together with miR‐21‐5p and miR‐145‐5p inhibits fibroblast movement and proliferation, whereas activates cell differentiation and senescence (Liang et al., 2016).

claim: miR-34a/c were specifically upregulated in VU, whereas their levels during wound repair remained relatively low and stable.
source: In this study, we described that miR-34a/c were specifically upregulated in VU, whereas their levels during wound repair remained relatively low and stable, suggesting their specific role in wound pathology.

source: Similarly, in the cell cycle pathway, miR-34a-5p directly targeted CCND1, CDK6, HDAC1, and E2F3, while miR-424-5p targeted ANAPC13, CCNE1, CDC25B, CDK1, CDKN1B, CHK1, WEE1, and YWHAH, and only CDC23 was cotargeted by both miRs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by microarray analysis and pathway mapping

source: In particular, both miRs enhanced keratinocyte expression of inflammatory chemokines/ cytokines, for example, CCL20, CXCL8, and IL1B (Figure 8f).

claim: The study collected wound-edge tissues from human acute wounds and chronic nonhealing VUs.
source: To better understand tissue repair in humans, we collected wound-edge tissues from human acute wounds and chronic nonhealing VUs (Figure 1a and Materials and methods, Tables 2 and 3).

source: In total, 20 samples divided into four groups, that is, Skin, Wound1, Wound7, and VU, were analyzed by Illumina small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) and ribosomal RNA-depleted long RNA sequencing (RNA-seq).
